title: 1968–1981: Running in Place
tagline: Bretton Woods collapses · Two oil crises · Thirteen years of stagflation · Keynesianism loses credibility

sections.heading: Era Tone
body: This is the chapter of US equities that 'leaves a bad taste' — the Dow Jones Industrial Average essentially ran in place for thirteen years. Bretton Woods began unraveling in 1968 (the two-tier gold system) and collapsed entirely in 1971 (the Nixon Shock). Two oil crises hit in 1973 and 1979, and 'stagflation' became the defining word for the US economy throughout the 1970s. The NBER identified four recessions in this stretch. Monthly year-over-year growth in industrial production fell to an average of 2.7% — half the prior decade's pace.

The key paradox: from 1969 to 1981, aggregate corporate earnings for US listed companies grew nearly 170%, yet the market PE fell from 18.1x at the end of 1968 to 8.1x at the end of 1981 (−55.5%). Earnings more than doubled, valuations were halved, and the index went nowhere — a textbook case of valuation compression.

The era ended with Reagan taking office in 1981 and Paul Volcker pushing the discount rate to 14%. Thirteen years had thoroughly destroyed the credibility of Keynesian economics, and supply-side economics and monetarism took the stage.

items.strong: 1969–1972: Stagflation Emerges and Bretton Woods Falls
items.body: Q4 1970 GDP slipped 0.2% year-over-year into a mild recession, yet core CPI was still 6.3% — 'stagflation' had formally arrived. On August 15, 1971, the Nixon Shock suspended dollar-gold convertibility, imposed wage and price controls, and added a 10% import surcharge. Bretton Woods was over. Price controls briefly suppressed inflation in 1971–1972, and 1972 GDP grew 5.3%.

The OPEC embargo of October 1973 sent oil from about $3 to about $12. 1974 GDP fell 0.5% and CPI hit 11%; energy contributed 11 percentage points to CPI and food 51 percentage points. 1974 was one of the worst years for US equities since the Great Depression (S&P 500 down 29.7%).

The 1975 recession bottomed, and the Tax Reduction Act of 1975 helped restart consumer spending. GDP went −0.2% in 1975 → +5.4% in 1976 → +4.6% in 1977 → +5.5% in 1978. But inflation never went away: CPI returned to 9.0% in 1978, forcing the Fed to hike seven times that year, taking the discount rate from 6% to 9.5%.

items.strong: 1979–1981: The Second Oil Crisis and the Volcker Tightening
items.body: The 1979 Iranian Revolution triggered a second oil crisis and CPI surged to 13.3%. Volcker took over the Fed in August 1979. 1980 brought recession with CPI at 13.5%. Volcker hiked decisively: the discount rate hit 13% in February 1980 and peaked at 14% in mid-1981. Reagan took office in 1981 and rolled out his Economic Recovery program (tax cuts plus spending discipline plus tight money).

sections.heading: Economic Structure: Deindustrialization Begins
body: The 1970s marked the beginning of US manufacturing offshoring. Manufacturing value added fell from 25% of GDP in 1968 to 20% in 1981 — a five-point decline far faster than the prior two decades. Three drivers: (1) lower-cost emerging economies (Japan, Western Europe, and the Asian Tigers); (2) falling global shipping costs; and (3) two energy-cost shocks from the oil crises.

Finance and real estate moved up: by 1981 the sector was 16% of GDP (+2pp), surpassing wholesale and retail (13%) and government spending (14%) for the first time to take second place. The tertiary sector broadened across the board: business services 6%, education and health 5%, and the information industry made its first appearance.

Inside manufacturing, petroleum/coal and computer/electronics were the only two sub-sectors growing faster than GDP (annualized nominal 14.3% and 10.5%), with traditional manufacturing lagging. Autos and parts and other transportation equipment posted annualized profit growth of −2.4% and −27.2% — autos were entering a prolonged decline.
Overseas profits' share rose from 9.3% to 14.4%, and multinational logic began to dominate the earnings structure of large companies. This foreshadowed the 'multinational giants' era of the 1980s.

sections.heading: Taxes: A Series of Cuts That Failed
body: The US effective corporate tax rate fell from 38% in 1969 to 25% in 1981 — a 13-point decline and the fastest postwar tax-cut cycle. Highlights: Nixon's Alternative Minimum Tax of 1969 broadened the base; Carter's 1978 cuts; and Reagan's 1981 Economic Recovery Tax Act (ERTA).

But tax cuts did little against stagflation: with inflation out of control, nominal profit gains were offset by falling real purchasing power, and 'fiscal drag' on households and businesses meant the progressive income tax silently raised real burdens.

items.body: The Washington Agreement between the US and seven Western European countries left the $35/oz official price in name only; Bretton Woods began to unravel.
items.title: Two-Tier Gold System

items.body: Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated on April 4, triggering riots in over a hundred American cities; Robert Kennedy was assassinated on June 5.
items.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Assassinated

items.body: On July 20, Neil Armstrong walked on the moon — a US comeback in the Cold War space race.
items.title: Apollo 11 Moon Landing

items.body: The gold window was closed, a 10% import surcharge imposed, and a 90-day wage-price freeze announced. Bretton Woods formally ended.
items.title: Nixon Shock

items.body: Nixon visited China February 21–28 and signed the Shanghai Communiqué, reshaping the Cold War order.
items.title: Nixon Visits China

items.body: The OPEC embargo quadrupled international oil prices.
items.title: First Oil Crisis

items.body: Nixon resigned on August 8 and Ford took office — one of the most serious constitutional crises in US history.
items.title: Watergate Resignation

items.body: Saigon fell on April 30 and the last US forces withdrew.
items.title: End of the Vietnam War

items.body: Bicentennial celebrations on July 4; Carter was elected president that year.
items.title: US Bicentennial

items.body: The Shah fled, Khomeini returned, and Iranian oil production halted; the Tehran embassy hostage crisis began on November 4 and lasted 444 days.
items.title: Iranian Revolution and the November Hostage Crisis

items.body: A serious blow to the US civilian nuclear industry.
items.title: Three Mile Island Accident

items.body: The 'Volcker Moment' began — using a 19% fed funds rate to crush inflation.
items.title: Volcker Becomes Fed Chair

items.body: Operation Eagle Claw failed and the Carter administration's standing collapsed.
items.title: Desert One Failure

items.body: Reagan's first executive order deregulated oil prices; the same day, the 444-day hostage crisis ended.
items.title: Reagan Inaugurated and Hostages Released

items.body: Reagan was shot outside the Washington Hilton on March 30 and survived.
items.title: Reagan Assassination Attempt

items.body: Reagan dismissed 11,345 striking air traffic controllers — the symbolic end of the unions' postwar golden age.
items.title: PATCO Strike
